clue.text: Well-built animal accommodation is over middle of docks

indicators.note: to be over something is to cover it on all sides, so one piece is wrapped around the other

parts.note: a sty is the pen where pigs are kept

indicators.note: the middle of something is its central part, so only the inner letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the central letters of the word, dropping the first and last

explanation.surface: A sturdy animal shed sits overlooking the centre of a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well-built' looks like it describes the accommodation, but it is the definition; 'over' here means covering, not above.
explanation.definitionFit: A stocky person has a solid, thickset frame, which is what calling someone well-built means.

clue.text: Deliver fixed charge crossing river…

indicators.note: something crossing a path cuts through the middle of it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a set fee is a fixed price
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Someone hands over a flat fee for a ferry across a river, and the dots carry on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: R slips inside FEE, the second word of SET FEE. The trailing dots only link the surface to 2 Down; the clues are solved separately.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver someone in the old sense is to rescue or release them, as in 'deliver us from evil'.

clue.text: …alternatively taking a little while to go round

parts.note: 'or' introduces an alternative
'wait a bit' means wait a little while

explanation.surface: Continuing from 1 Down, someone takes their time going the long way round.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots pick up from 1 Down only for the surface story. OR is followed by BIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Planets and satellites orbit when they travel in a repeating path around a larger body.

clue.text: Kuala Lumpur's protecting special trees for bird of prey

indicators.note: to protect is to shield on all sides, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: the first letters of the two words, the city's usual initials

indicators.note: something special is out of the ordinary, so these letters are put into an unusual order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Malaysia's capital is guarding some unusual trees for the sake of a hawk.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for 'is'. The rearranged trees sit between the K and the L of KL.
explanation.definitionFit: The kestrel is a small falcon that hovers before swooping, so it is one example of a raptor.

clue.text: Greys out bare behind in hot spring

indicators.note: 'out' can mean in disorder or wrong, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: the behind of something is its rear end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Pale figures with their bottoms exposed are hiding in a hot pool, a cheeky bathing scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bare behind' paints a naked bottom, but 'behind' just asks for the back letter of 'bare'. That letter joins GREYS before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A geyser is a natural spring that periodically shoots out boiling water and steam, as in Iceland.

clue.text: Rang City journalist blocked by Home Office

indicators.note: something blocked by an obstacle has that obstacle stuck in its middle

parts.note: EC is the postcode of the City of London, the financial district
HO is the abbreviation for the Home Office, the UK interior ministry
ED, short for editor, is the crossword's usual journalist

explanation.surface: A financial reporter telephoned but was stonewalled by the government department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rang' looks like making a phone call, but it is the sound sense. The City is London's financial district, whose postcode starts EC.
explanation.definitionFit: A hall or bell rang or echoed when sound resounded and reverberated through it, a past-tense synonym.

clue.text: Cry to drop rents

parts.note: trees shed or drop their leaves
a rent is a rip in fabric

explanation.surface: A tenant weeps on hearing that the rents are coming down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rents' reads as payments, but here it is the noun for rips, which are spelled the same as the drops from the eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: To cry is to weep, and weeping means letting teardrops fall from your eyes, the idiom.

clue.text: Saved special copper trapped by rampant animal

indicators.note: something trapped by a thing is caught inside it
a rampant beast rears up on its hind legs, and in a down clue rising up means reading upward

parts.note: a deer is a common animal
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
S is the standard abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: A police officer on special duty, cornered by a wild beast, was rescued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman, but it is the metal. 'Rampant' is a heraldic word for a beast rearing on its hind legs.
explanation.definitionFit: To rescue someone is to save them from danger, so the past tenses of the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Too many cases of overindulgence and back chat start to grate over time

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece over another simply sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: overindulgence is excess

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: gab is idle chat, as in the gift of the gab

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening, so only its first letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Over time, all the overeating and backchat start to irritate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back chat' looks like one word, cheek, but 'back' reverses 'chat'. 'Cases' in the definition are suitcases, not instances.
explanation.definitionFit: Excess baggage is luggage over the airline's weight allowance, so it means having too many suitcases.

clue.text: Try backing strikes

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the letters are read the other way

parts.note: a batter bats, or strikes, the ball

explanation.surface: Supporting a workers' walkout, or a rugby score backed by strikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strikes' could be stoppages; here it is the verb hits, which reverses into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a stab at something is an idiom for making an attempt, so it is a noun synonym of try.

clue.text: Feeling there's no reason for sexist being horrible about hens raving

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other
something horrible is a mess, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: raving means wild and out of control, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: There is no excuse for a sexist being nasty about a rowdy hen party.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate anagrams, one placed inside the other. 'Hens raving' suggests a hen party, a British pre-wedding night out for the bride and her friends.
explanation.definitionFit: A sixth sense is intuition: a hunch or perception that comes without logical grounds or evidence.

clue.text: Author's more genuine in conversation

indicators.note: conversation is spoken, so we want a word that is said the same as another

parts.note: more right, that is more genuine or correct

explanation.surface: A novelist seems more sincere when talking than on the page.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for 'is'. 'Righter' is an unusual comparative, but it is fair for more correct.
explanation.definitionFit: An author is someone who writes books, so the two are everyday synonyms.

clue.text: With lots going on day before, books mostly packed

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: the eve is the day before an event, as in Christmas Eve
NT, the New Testament, is a set of books of the Bible
full means packed, here without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone frantically busy the day before a trip, with the suitcase nearly packed with books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Books' is the usual crossword NT (or OT); here it is the New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: An eventful day is one full of incidents, so it is busy with happenings and activity.

clue.text: Severe crime's punished not so much

indicators.note: something punished is knocked about, so these letters are beaten into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
less means a smaller amount

explanation.surface: A complaint that serious crime is treated too leniently by the courts.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for 'is'. The surface argues for harsher sentences, and the answer is exactly what such critics want.
explanation.definitionFit: A merciless punishment shows no pity, so it is harsh and unsparing, a synonym of severe.

clue.text: Hushed up scam and dodgy deal involving church

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: a con is a swindle

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so these letters are twisted out of order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A fraud and a shady transaction involving the church were covered up.
explanation.walkthrough: The church abbreviation is placed in the deal first, and only then are the combined letters shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hushed up has been kept secret or hidden from view, which is what concealed means.

clue.text: Heavy cart reversed in area next to house

indicators.note: the letters are written in the opposite order

parts.note: a dray is a low cart for heavy loads, traditionally beer barrels

explanation.surface: Someone backs a heavy wagon into the space beside their home.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a reversing manoeuvre, which is exactly what happens to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A yard is an enclosed patch of ground beside a building, so it is land adjoining a dwelling.

clue.text: Support neutral replacing Conservative in financial institution

indicators.note: to replace one thing is to swap something else in for it

parts.note: to back someone is to support them
N is neutral, as on an electric plug or gear stick
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A political story: backing a non-aligned candidate instead of a Tory at the central bank.
explanation.walkthrough: In BACK the C is swapped for N. 'Conservative' and 'neutral' read as politics but are single letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank is a business that holds deposits and lends money, the standard example of one.

clue.text: Most daring items of underwear

parts.note: a bra is a woman's undergarment
in British English a vest is a sleeveless undershirt

explanation.surface: A lingerie shop's most risqué pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daring' suggests revealing underwear, but it is the definition; in British English a vest is a sleeveless undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: The bravest person shows the greatest courage, so it is the superlative of daring or bold.

clue.text: Fizzy drink stand with 20% off is splendid

indicators.note: a fifth of a five-letter word is one letter, so the last one is removed like a discount

parts.note: Fanta is an orange soft drink brand
to stick something is to stand or tolerate it, here missing its last letter

explanation.surface: A soft-drink stall offering a fifth off is excellent, like a shop sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' looks like a stall, but it is the verb tolerate, as in 'I can't stick it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fantastic is informal praise for something excellent or wonderful, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Crack shot hunter's framing head of deer

indicators.note: a frame goes around a picture, so one piece encloses another
shot can mean ruined or worn out, so these letters are broken up

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: the head of a word is its top, so only its first letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: An expert marksman lines up a stag's head in his sights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack shot' reads as an expert marksman, but the two words split: 'Crack' is the definition and 'shot' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A crack of thunder is the sharp loud noise that follows lightning, so crack names that sound.

clue.text: Enhance evidence supporting motorway going north

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece is underneath, so it comes after the other
north is up, and in a down clue travelling upward means reading the letters backwards

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, with the 1 read as I
to evidence a claim is to prove it

explanation.surface: Better traffic data justifying the northbound motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evidence' looks like a noun but is the verb. The M1 runs from London to Leeds; reversed it gives IM, placed above PROVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To enhance something is to make it better or raise its quality, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Prepared quite quietly before card game

indicators.note: one piece placed before another simply comes first in the line

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical marking for quietly

indicators.note: prepared food is chopped and made up, so these letters are worked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone got ready in silence before a round of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal leads the clue though its fodder comes second in the answer; P goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Piquet is an old two-player trick-taking game played with a 32-card pack, one example.

clue.text: Fish swallows superb white insect

indicators.note: whatever swallows something takes it inside itself

parts.note: the ling is a long sea fish of the cod family
ace means excellent
W is the abbreviation for white

explanation.surface: A fish gulps down a fine pale bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallows' could be birds, but it is the verb, and the fish does the swallowing.
explanation.definitionFit: The lacewing is a delicate insect with gauzy, net-veined wings, so it is one example of the class.

clue.text: Not ready for eating and travelling in Peru

indicators.note: travelling means moving about, so these letters move into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tourist in South America who is too busy touring to stop for food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Peru' looks like a location but its six letters are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Unripe fruit has not yet matured, so it is not ready to be eaten.

clue.text: Caught thievin' bird

indicators.note: to catch a remark is to hear it, so we want a word as it is heard

parts.note: thieving is robbing, and the apostrophe drops the final G as in casual speech

explanation.surface: Someone was nabbed while stealing, told in slangy dialect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like an arrest, but it means heard. The dropped G in thievin' tells you the sound is clipped too.
explanation.definitionFit: The robin is a small red-breasted songbird, one example of a bird and a famous garden species.

clue.text: Considered getting married to receive students' rate

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: to be wed is to be married
L is a learner or student, so two of them give two Ls
to rate something is to assess or judge it

explanation.surface: Someone weighs up marrying in order to get the student discount.
explanation.walkthrough: A learner is L, from the L-plate on a British learner driver's car, so plural students give two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A considered decision has been carefully thought through, which is what a well-judged one is.

clue.text: Lad picked up danger sign at sea

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so we want a word as it is heard

parts.note: a lad is a young male

explanation.surface: A boy is rescued from the water after spotting a warning signal.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech the floating marker is usually said the same as boy; in America it often rhymes with 'chewy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A buoy is a moored float that marks hazards such as rocks or shallows for ships.

clue.text: Until now you'd regularly popped into art gallery

indicators.note: something popped into a place is put inside it

parts.note: the Tate is the famous London art gallery

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that up till now you would often drop into the museum.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is London's national gallery of modern and British art; OD goes inside it after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: So far or up to the present moment is what 'to date' means, an idiom of time.

clue.text: British taking on French eleven for third place

indicators.note: to take something on is to add it, so one piece is attached after the other

parts.note: BR is the abbreviation for British
onze is French for eleven

explanation.surface: A British side plays a French football team in the third-place play-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eleven' suggests a team, but it is just the number, in French.
explanation.definitionFit: The bronze medal is awarded to whoever finishes third, so the metal stands for that position.
